summary: Menadione sodium bisulfite is a water-soluble derivative of menadione (synthetic vitamin K3, a provitamin K). After absorption it is converted in the body toward active forms of vitamin K, which is an essential cofactor for the hepatic gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and of proteins C and S. It was used historically as a vitamin K source for vitamin K deficiency and hypoprothrombinemic states. Critically, menadione (vitamin K3) is NOT used in neonates or infants because it causes hemolytic anemia, hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus, and it can precipitate hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency; for these reasons phytonadione (vitamin K1) replaced it for neonatal and most human use. It is largely obsolete and not FDA-approved for human use in the US (encountered mainly as an animal-feed additive and in some non-US supplements). This record is based on historical monograph/pharmacology sources.

moa: Menadione (vitamin K3) is a synthetic provitamin that is converted in the body toward biologically active vitamin K. Vitamin K acts as an essential cofactor for the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which post-translationally gamma-carboxylates glutamate residues on clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X and on the anticoagulant proteins C and S, rendering them functional. Replenishing vitamin K therefore restores synthesis of functional clotting factors and corrects vitamin K deficiency hypoprothrombinemia. Unlike phytonadione, the menadione nucleus can also act as an oxidant, which underlies its capacity to cause hemolysis (especially in neonates and G6PD deficiency).

preg: Avoid, particularly near term and during labor: menadione (vitamin K3) can cause hemolysis, hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus in the newborn. If vitamin K is required in pregnancy, phytonadione (vitamin K1) is the appropriate choice.
lact: Avoid. Menadione can provoke hemolysis and hyperbilirubinemia in the infant; phytonadione (vitamin K1) is preferred where maternal or infant vitamin K supplementation is needed.
renal: No specific established dosage adjustment for renal impairment; data are limited given its obsolete human use. Monitor for hemolysis as oxidative stress and reduced clearance could increase risk.
hepatic: Vitamin K (including menadione-derived activity) is less effective when severe hepatocellular disease prevents synthesis of clotting factors; in that setting failure of the prothrombin time to correct points to hepatic synthetic failure rather than simple vitamin K deficiency.

major: Vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants (warfarin, acenocoumarol) - menadione/vitamin K antagonizes their effect and can cause loss of anticoagulation
moderate: Drugs causing oxidative stress - additive hemolysis risk, especially in G6PD deficiency
Bile-acid sequestrants / orlistat - reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K (less relevant for this water-soluble form)
minor: Broad-spectrum antibiotics - may alter gut vitamin K production and baseline status
interactions.food: As a water-soluble derivative, absorption is not dependent on dietary fat (unlike fat-soluble vitamin K1).
interactions.diagnostics: Corrects/normalizes a prolonged prothrombin time/INR caused by vitamin K deficiency; hemolysis can raise bilirubin and reticulocyte counts.

common: Generally limited data; gastrointestinal upset reported with oral vitamin K3 forms
serious: Hemolytic anemia (especially neonates and G6PD deficiency)
Hypersensitivity reactions, including to the bisulfite component
rare: Injection-site reactions where parenteral forms were used

counsel: This is an older synthetic form of vitamin K (vitamin K3) that has largely been replaced by vitamin K1 (phytonadione)
It must never be given to newborns or infants because it can cause dangerous breakdown of red cells and jaundice
Tell your clinician if you have G6PD deficiency or a sulfite allergy before any vitamin K3 product
Report yellowing of the skin/eyes, dark urine, unusual tiredness or breathlessness (signs of red-cell breakdown)
If you take a blood thinner such as warfarin, vitamin K can reduce its effect - do not take it without advice

pearls: Not FDA-approved for human use in the US and largely obsolete - encountered mainly as an animal-feed additive and in some non-US supplements; record based on historical monograph/pharmacology sources
CRITICAL: never use in neonates or infants - causes hemolytic anemia, hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus, which is why phytonadione (vitamin K1) replaced it
Can precipitate oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Vitamin K3 (menadione) differs from fat-soluble K1 - it is water-soluble and does not need bile/dietary fat for absorption
Like all vitamin K, it antagonizes warfarin-type anticoagulants
missed: For a historical supplemental regimen, a missed dose could generally be taken when remembered unless close to the next scheduled dose, in which case the missed dose is skipped - never double up. Given its obsolete status, dosing decisions should follow current clinical guidance, which favors phytonadione (vitamin K1).
overdose: Excessive menadione (vitamin K3) is associated chiefly with hemolysis, hyperbilirubinemia and (in susceptible patients/neonates) kernicterus, rather than thrombosis. Management is supportive: stop the drug, monitor hemoglobin and bilirubin, provide transfusion or exchange transfusion for severe hemolysis/neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and treat any hypersensitivity reaction. In a patient on a vitamin K antagonist, excess vitamin K can cause warfarin resistance requiring alternative anticoagulation.
